analytic.title: Recent advances and future prospects of thermochemical biofuel conversion processes with machine learning

div.p: Biofuels have been widely recognized as potential solutions to addressing the climate crisis and strengthening energy security and sustainability. However, techno-economic and environmental challenges for the production of biofuels remain and complicated conversion processes and factors, such as materials and process design, need to be taken into consideration for solving the challenges, which is not easy. Machine Learning (ML) has been combined with the theories of thermochemical biofuel conversion processes to achieve accurate and efficient biofuel process modelling. In this review, existing ML applications to predict biofuel yield and composition are critically reviewed. The details of the input and output variables of the developed models for thermochemical biofuel conversion processes were summarized, and their development procedures were compared. Techno-economic analysis results incorporating ML applications in biofuels were also reviewed. Although developed models in literature showed good performance for their targets, respectively, they can hardly be applied to other feedstocks or operating conditions. To overcome the challenge and develop universal model, perspective approaches were suggested in this study. It was suggested that it is essential to develop systematic datasets to support more comprehensive machine learning-based modelling towards practical applications. Potential prospective research and development directions on machine learning-based thermochemical biofuel conversion process modeling were recommended, so that it can assist in the commercialization and optimization of various biofuel conversions leading to a sustainable and circular society.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The utilization of renewable energy sources, including biomass, has increased worldwide to reduce an increase in the amount of greenhouse gases resulting in severe environmental challenges [1][2][3].

Among the various renewable resources, biomass including lignocellulosic and municipal wastes is unique in that it has been used for a long time, even in conventional energy systems and has received considerable interest for a few decades as a reliable alternative to fossil fuel [4]. The amount of power generated by biomass combustion reached 750 TWh in 2021, and the supply from biomass is expected to increase to 100 EJ by 2050 [5,6]. The development of biomass energy conversion processes, based on e.g., biochemical and thermochemical methods, has been increasing in recent years owing to their low-emission characteristics, among other advantages [5,7,8]. In particular, biofuels have the potential to contribute to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UNSDGs) by promoting affordable and clean energy (Goal 7), industry, innovation, and infrastructure (Goal 9), responsible consumption and production (Goal 12), and climate action (Goal 13) [9].

Biomass conversion processes, either biochemical or thermochemical, allow fuels, heat, electricity, and other value-added products to be produced. The biochemical conversion process utilizes bacteria, enzymes, and microorganisms to break down biomass into fuel and other products [10][11][12]. The main drawback of biochemical processes is their low reaction rate, owing to which hours, days, or weeks are usually required to complete the necessary reactions. In contrast, thermochemical conversion processes rather utilize thermal energy sources and chemical reactions to decompose biomass into various products [13][14][15]. Compared to biochemical processes, thermochemical processes are relatively fast, as reactions can occur within a few minutes or even seconds. They are also suitable for wider ranges of feedstocks [16].

Thermochemical conversion has been the most widely used method owing to its advantages and high conversion efficiency [2,17]. They can be grouped into torrefaction [18], pyrolysis [19,20], gasification [21], and hydrothermal treatments [22]. Torrefaction is conducted at low temperatures (<320 • C) under the absence of oxygen or partial oxidizing gas in order to upgrade the fuel characteristics [18]. Pyrolysis is the thermal treatment of biomass under an inert environment to produce liquid biofuels, gases, and solid residues. Depending on the heating rate and residence time, pyrolysis is generally divided into slow, fast, and flash pyrolysis [23,24]. The efficacy and quality of pyrolysis products greatly depend on the heating rate, temperature, feedstock particle size, residence time, and moisture content [25,26].

Pretreatment of feedstock also plays a role in the process, as depicted by the increasing pyrolytic gas yield with HCl pretreatment [27]. Gasification involves the conversion of biomass to syngas under a condition with a limited oxygen supply [4,14,28]. It can be classified into conventional and hydrothermal types depending on the type of gasifying agent, reaction conditions, and quality of the produced syngas [2,29]. Unlike other thermochemical technologies that normally favor dry biomass, hydrothermal treatment can transform wet biomass into gases, solid fuels, and other constituents at reasonable energy efficiencies. Hydrothermal treatment involves the utilization of hot pressurized water as a reactant to produce biofuels [17]. It can be classified as either hydrothermal carbonation or hydrothermal liquefaction, based on the temperature, pressure, and proportions of the converted intermediate products [30]. The design of these processes presents various challenges, mostly owing to their multiparametric and complex characteristics. In addition, serious consideration should be given to catalyst [31], in terms of basic properties [32] that increased the yield of oil and gas while that of char is suppressed [33].

Typical thermochemical conversion research often requires rigorous experiments to determine the optimal design and operation [5,12]. Over the years, novel modeling techniques, including computational fluid dynamics (CFD), kinetic and thermodynamic models, and process models, have been employed to accelerate process optimization while reducing operation time and cost [34][35][36][37][38].

However, modeling using these conventional techniques is sometimes unrealistic and difficult [39,40]. This is because these models are based on a variety of assumptions, either elaborated or oversimplified, affecting the quality of the model predictions and/or leading to great difficulty in implementation [41].

In addition, these models are difficult to incorporate under different operating conditions [36,42]. For example, CFD is time-consuming and computationally expensive because it requires a significant amount of processing power and predefined engine-specific parameters [37,38]. Therefore, developing an accurate, non-time-consuming, non-computationally expensive, and robust modeling approach to model the processes is of utmost importance.

Machine Learning (ML) techniques have proven to be reliable alternatives to the traditional modeling techniques for studying and comprehending complex conversion processes. They can model complex problems by leveraging a series of interconnections between the input and output parameters. Recently, the application of ML approaches to model thermochemical biofuel conversion processes have increased significantly. The applications include the prediction of the yield and composition of products, kinetic parameters, and calorific values of the products. The ML models developed have also been used to determine the optimal conditions for desired production. The preprocessing or normalization of input variables with distinctive magnitudes is a hyperparameter that contributes to improve the performance of machine learning-based models. However, some did not state the measures adopted to prevent overfitting, which is a crucial challenge against the model improvement [38,[43][44][45].

Previous reviews summarized the ML application of biomass conversion processes, where specific datasets (e.g., not diverse type of feedstock and operating conditions) were utilized. The developed ML models showed good performance, but extrapolation or further improvement of the ML model was limited by the variability in the conversion process such as types of reactors, feedstocks, and operating conditions. In real applications, the development of a universal ML model is necessary to produce biofuel stably regardless of the condition of biomass feedstock. As a first step to develop such universal model, the variability in the dimensions of the dataset, as well as the number of data points, were compared in this study. Preprocessing and the possibility of overfitting in the developed ML are also discussed. Then, this review summarized the results of estimating the importance of input variables in individual ML models in order to discuss which input variables are important. Finally, relevant challenges in the development of universal ML model are summarized and potential solutions and future research directions are suggested.

div.head: General overview of machine learning
div.p: Machine learning methods can be classified as supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised, or reinforcement learning. In supervised learning methods, labeled input and output datasets are used for the training and validation of the model. The model then learns to map the input data to its targeted output [46]. Supervised learning methods can be categorized into regression and classification methods.
Classification methods seek to identify behavioral patterns across datasets, whereas regression methods aim to establish the best match between the input and output parameters [47].

In contrast to supervised learning, unsupervised machine learning, also known as self-organization, works best with unlabeled data and is excellent at detecting any possible hidden patterns. As input data are fed into an unsupervised ML model, the model seeks and classifies the similarities and differences between the data accordingly. Examples of unsupervised ML include principal component analysis, dimensionality reduction, and clustering. Semi-supervised learning combines the advantages of supervised and unsupervised learning. It aids in the resolution of supervised learning challenges and can handle systems with both unlabeled and labeled inputs [46]. It is worth noting that labeling data for supervised learning is often difficult and time-consuming. Semi-supervised learning can overcome this drawback by incorporating a portion of the total unlabeled input into the supervised learning process [46,48].

The last class of ML algorithms, reinforcement learning, involves a learning system called an agent, which understands its environment through a series of actions that could give it a reward or penalty. A positive action yields rewards and negative action results in a penalty. The agent allows a better understanding of its environment without human intervention, based on maximizing profit and reducing penalties [49,50]. Some prominent ML algorithms employed in the field of science and engineering, which can be implemented for biomass thermochemical conversion processes, are presented in Fig. 1.

div.head: Several ML algorithms have been utilized for different aspects of biomass thermochemical conversion
div.p: processes. The most widely explored algorithms are artificial neural networks (ANN). Other less popular algorithms include decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, deep neural networks, and hybrid intelligent models. A brief discussion of ANN and other algorithms that have been used in various applications of this field have been given by Umenweke et al. [2], Ascher et al. [26],
Ascher et al. [51], and Shahbeik et al. [29]. More explanation about methods to estimate feature importance was added to Supplementary Material.

div.head: Machine Learning (ML) applications in thermochemical biofuel conversion processes
div.p: Thermochemical conversion processes convert biomass resources into various biofuels such as hydrogen, methane, biogas, bio-oil and biochar. To maximize the selectivity or yield of biofuel and the conversion efficiency, various ML approaches have been applied to the thermochemical biofuel conversion processes. Before applying ML methods, the performance of a trained model needs to be assessed using the test dataset acquired from thermochemical biofuel conversion processes. Most studies describe the performance of models using a correlation coefficient (R 2 ) or root mean square error, which is sufficient for a single-output model. However, in the case of a multioutput model, the performance of model should consider the different magnitudes of each output, and the role of R 2 should be limited to evaluating the correlation of each output. Thus, for multioutput models, relative measures, such as the average percentage error or root relative squared error, are recommended to compare the averaged performance of different models.

It is important to know how the prediction of ML models could deviate from experimental values, but few studies provided the respective yield values in ML studies. Instead, some studies provided the averaged percentage error between experimental value and prediction. This could better indicate how different the predicted values are from the experiment on average. In addition, it is also important that the distribution of deviations (differences between experiment results and predicted values) should be scattered uniformly regardless of the magnitude of the experimental value. Thus, the deviations of all experimental values should be investigated rather than specific values. Some ML models showed relatively poor correlation (R 2 <0.9), implying underfit of the models.

There are various methods to increase the R 2 value, and the first method is to increase the number of available data. In addition, the selection of effective input variables can be another method. Many studies did so, and the best combination of input variables for a given system was suggested. It should be noted that a high R 2 value doesn't assess whether overfitting occurs. Thus, methods to prevent overfitting, such as the early stop method or regularization method, should be used. Considering these aspects, the detailed procedure for the model development is summarized in the following section. The detailed description of the configuration of the ML model can help to reproduce the developed ML models, and it can be found in the references.

div.head: Yield and composition of products under dry conditions
div.p: Generally, the condition of biomass used in thermochemical biofuel conversion processes can be divided into dry and wet conditions, depending on whether external water is added to the conversion processes. The moisture content of the biomass used in those processes was neglected for the classification of the processes. The yield and composition of biomass thermochemical conversion products depend on feedstock characteristics (e.g., proximate and ultimate compositions) and operating conditions, such as temperature, residence time, and heating rate under dry condition [25]. They are also the main input variables used in existing ML-based models. ML-based models with ultimate composition data showed better performance than that with proximate composition data when the same dataset was used in both cases [52]. However, the performance of ML-based models was significantly improved when both composition data were included as input variables [52]. It should be noted that the chemical and structural composition of biomass resources depends on the types of feedstocks [53]. In the case of algal feedstock, the major components are carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins, whereas those of lignocellulose feedstock are hemicellulose, lignin, and cellulose [53][54][55]. Thus, some studies have also included the content of the major components as input variables for ML model development. The particle size of the biomass was also used as an input variable [28]. In the case of the operating conditions, the temperature, heating rate, retention time, and gas velocity were utilized as input variables.

The yield and composition of products and byproducts are typical output variables for ML-based models. The yield can be calculated as the ratio of the target product mass to the feedstock mass. When various combinations of input variables were tested, a R 2 value was reached to 0.862 [56][57][58]. Onsree et al. developed a model incorporating operating environments (N 2 , O 2 , and CO 2 ) and showed high performance for predicting biochar yield (R 2 > 0.915) using datasets with 10 types of feedstocks [59].

The performance of models for predicting the elemental composition and carbon content of biochar ranged from R 2 = 0.66 [56] to R 2 =0.8480 [58]. A higher heating value (HHV) is the calorific value of the fuel associated with quality [60]. For the prediction of the HHV of biochar, a R 2 value of 0.9052 was achieved by Onsree et al. [59].

For predicting the yield of bio-oil per biomass, a R 2 value of 0.95 was achieved by the ML model of Ullah et al. [61]. The yield of water, a liquid-phase byproduct produced during thermochemical conversion, was also predicted by ML models [62,63]. The ML prediction of the composition of biooil produced under dry conditions is yet to be reported, which might be attributed to the fact that there are insufficient datasets in dry conditions. H 2 , CO, CO 2 , and CH 4 are major gas species that evolve from thermochemical conversion and their yields have been commonly considered as the outputs of ML models [64,65]. Yucel et al. used various datasets with different feedstock types to develop ML models for predicting the total gas yield and gas composition of biomass gasification [65]. The performance for the total gas yield and for the gas compositions of H 2 , CO, CO 2 , and CH 4 were indicated by R 2 = 0.86, 0.85, respectively. Tang et al. developed a ML model to predict the yields of H 2 , CO, CO 2 , and CH 4 with an R 2 value of 0.999 [64].

The model was developed using a relatively large amount of data (3831 data points), but only two feedstocks were used, implying the necessity for further validation of other feedstocks. Ascher [52]. The total gas yield, cold gas efficiency, and carbon conversion efficiency were also predicted in this study. ML models have also been developed to predict other output variables such as the total gas yield [57,62,66], HHV [65], lower heating value (LHV) [52,66], H 2 composition [43], CO/CO 2 composition [62], and the maximum yields of H 2 , CO, and CH 4 [28]. Additionally, the tar concentration in syngas and total tar yield (per biomass mass) were also predicted based on the development of ML models [67]. The LHV of byproducts produced in dry thermochemical conversion was predicted well, with R 2 = 0.988 [66].

A few studies have included different gas environments under dry conditions as input variables for ML model development. Zhao et al. included the O 2 composition in gas as an input variable (predictor), and the yields of biochar, biogas, tar, and water were simultaneously predicted [62]. Onsree et al.

included the composition of N 2 , CO 2 , and O 2 in a gaseous environment as input variables, and the yield and HHV of the solid product were predicted [59]. A summary of the ML models used to predict the yield and composition of products under dry conditions is presented in Table 1.

As mentioned above, the inclusion of both proximate and ultimate compositions as input variables usually led to good ML modelling performance. However, different forms of composition-based input variables were utilized. For example, some studies consider ultimate composition in as ratio form, such as the hydrogen/carbon ratio (H/C) and oxygen/carbon ratio (O/C). When various forms of input variables were tested during model development, the performance in the ratio form was better than that of the composition itself [56]. The O/C ratio is reported to be a good measure of carbohydrate, lipid, and protein levels in algae [74]. The yield of bio-oil mainly depends on the fraction of carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins, with lipids as the most significant factor, followed by proteins and carbohydrates [74,75]. A low H/C value in biomass could indicate a large fraction of lignin and a small fraction of hemicellulose [59]. In addition, the O/C and N/C ratios in biochar could be indicators of the polarity of biochar, as well as its surface properties [76]. In the case of lignocellulose biomass, high O/C and H/C ratios imply high fractions of hemicellulose and cellulose and low lignin fractions [53]. These studies have shown that the ratio of elements can better describe specific component (e.g., lignin or hemicellulose), which determines the mechanism of thermochemical conversion of biomass. This implies that choosing the elemental ratios as input variables can be beneficial for ML development.

Hence, it is recommended that the component ratio form that describes the determining factor of thermochemical mechanism is applied for ML development. If such mechanisms are not well known, a systematic search for a ratio form with better performance might shed light on the thermochemical conversion mechanism of biomass.

div.head: Conversion kinetics and kinetic parameters under dry conditions
div.p: Artificial neural networks and random forest have been widely applied to predict the kinetics or kinetic parameters such as the activation energy and pre-exponential factor of the thermochemical conversion of biomass. In addition, thermal gravimetric mass loss of biomass upon heating has been widely predicted using ML models.

Biomass composition was used as an input variable to predict the activation energy of pyrolysis under dry conditions, which was calculated based on various estimation methods such as Kissinger-Akahira-Sunose, Ozawa-Flynn-Wall, and Friedman methods) [53]. Based on the data of thermogravimetric analysis, the fractions of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin of various biomass have been used to predict the reaction kinetic parameters, such as the pre-exponential factor (log k 0 ), activation energy

(log E a ), and reaction order (log n) [72]. Similar results were obtained for the heating rate used to predict the activation energy of pyrolysis [73]. The time series of mass loss upon algal pyrolysis in an argon environment was predicted using the heating rate, initial temperature, and target temperature of the system [71].

Wei et al. developed a ML model to predict the thermal gravimetric mass-loss curve for the cocombustion of biomass and coal [74]. The input variables included the composition of biomass and coal and their blending ratio and operating parameters, such as heating rate and temperature. The importance of the input variables was as follows: temperature > blending ratio of biomass and coal > composition of biomass and coal > heating rate. A summary of the ML models for predicting the conversion kinetics and kinetic parameters of thermochemical conversion under dry conditions is presented in Table 2.

div.head: Yield and composition of products under wet conditions
div.p: Similar to dry conditions, the prediction of the yield, composition, and properties of solid products (called biochar) produced under wet conditions has been widely studied using various ML models.

Under wet conditions, the reactant or water is the supplementary factor for the conversion process. A few studies have included reactant information, such as reactant-to-biomass ratio (or biomass-toreactant ratio), as input variables [75][76][77][78].

Although the biomass-to-water ratio was included as an input variable in these studies [75,76,79], its importance to yield was estimated to be low. The composition of biochar was predicted with diverse output variables, such as carbon content (or carbon recovery) [45,80,81], nitrogen content [79], inorganic phosphorus content [81], atomic ratios [75,80], and ash content of the solid product [75]. Wei et al. predicted the H/C and O/C ratios of solid products before and after the reaction to estimate the product quality [82]. This was based on the fact that energy loss during combustion was lower for the biochar with lower H/C and O/C ratios [83]. The energy recovery and HHV of biochar were predicted using ML models [45,75,80]. In these studies, temperature and retention time were commonly included as input variables; however, different combinations of biomass characteristics were used. In the case of liquid products, higher efforts than under dry conditions are involved in developing ML models for the prediction of yield and composition of bio-oil [45,76,77,84] and byproducts (aqueous co-product) [45,76]. The elemental composition of the bio-oil (C, H, O, N, and S) was predicted [76], and the same was true for the specific composition of C, N, and O [45,85], energy recovery [45] and HHV [76,77] of the bio-oil. When a dataset with various types of reactants and catalysts was used to develop ML models, the types of reactants and catalysts were designated as categorical input variables [77].

Product gases with various compositions and yields produced under wet conditions were predicted using various ML models. The output variables of the developed models included the yield of total produced gas [39,45,76,85], the yield of H 2 , CH 4 , CO 2 , CO, C 2 H 4 , and C 2 H 6 [78,86], and the pollution index (CO 2 +CO) [77]. Notably, most ML models include biomass-to-water or biomass-to-reactant ratios as predictors. The distributions of biochar, syngas, and tar were well predicted by the models with good performance (R 2 > 0.91) [78]. It was shown that the effect of biomass characteristics was more pronounced for predicting biochar production, whereas temperature was more pronounced for predicting syngas and tar production. In addition, the reactant-to-biomass ratio is an important input variable for the CO 2 fraction in syngas, but not for other gases [78]. A summary of the ML models for predicting the yield and composition of products under wet conditions is presented in Table 3.

div.head: MDI
div.p: GBR was the best model. Relative importance was as follow.

Char production: AC>C>O (80% total importance) Syngas production: N>C>T(70% total importance) Two optimal models were used to find optimal operating condition for H2 production [78] Functional groups containing oxygen and hydrogen in biomass are detached from the structure through decarboxylation and dehydration during the thermochemical conversion of mass under wet conditions [93]. Thus, the changes in the O/C and H/C ratios in biochar can represent the extent of dehydration and decarboxylation during thermochemical conversion, respectively. Mu et al. defined indices for the decarboxylation degree (DCD) and dehydration degree (DHD), which are the ratios of O/C and H/C ratios before and after the reaction [75]. The smaller the value of the indices, the stronger the decarboxylation and dehydration reactions that occur during thermochemical conversion, and and the higher quality of solid fuel [75]. These indices were predicted using ML models with temperature as the most important input variable. The O content and ash content in the biomass were the subsequent important factors for DCD and DHD, respectively. The use of output variables, such as DCD and DHD, for ML modelling was shown to achieve improved performance and dimensional extrapolability [94].

In addition, dimensional extrapolation ca markedly reduce the number of experiments required to develop an ML model [95]. Thus, DCD and DHD are recommended to be considered for modelling biomass conversion processes under wet conditions.

div.head: Comparison of the relative importance of input variables on prediction
div.p: A comparison of the relative importance of the input variables on the predictive performance of ML models is presented in Tables 4 and5. During the estimation of the importance, input variables were simply categorized into feedstock characteristics and operating conditions while the importance of categorical variable was eliminated. Feedstock characteristics included elemental composition, elemental ratio, proximate analysis, and the fraction of lignin, hemicellulose, and cellulose of biomass.

The operating conditions included all input variables except for the feedstock characteristics, including blending ratio and particle size. As shown in Table 4, the contribution of feedstock characteristics to syngas compositions under dry conditions varies across studies: the number of studies with feedstock characteristics having higher importance and that with operating conditions was 9:8 under dry conditions, implying equal contributions. Under wet conditions, the contribution of operating conditions was larger than that of feedstock characteristics (Table 5). For the yield, composition, and calorific value of biochar under wet conditions, the contribution of feedstock characteristics was larger than that of operating conditions. Similarly, the contribution of feedstock characteristics to the yield and composition of bio-oil was large. The number of studies with feedstock characteristics having higher importance and that for operating conditions was 17:5 under wet conditions, implying an extremely high contribution of the feedstock characteristics. The histograms of the relative importance of feedstock characteristics on the ML models are plotted in Figs 2 (a) -(c). In the case of dry conditions, the distribution was left-skewed, showing that the number of models with low importance of feedstock characteristics was large. However, in the case of the wet conditions, the distribution was right-skewed as the number of models with a high importance of feedstock characteristics was more. This could be attributed to the fact that compared to dry conditions, wet conditions include a wide range of operating conditions, such as catalyst and reactant types. Such operating conditions were designated as categorical input variables, but their contributions were eliminated during the summation of relative importance, leading to a decreased contribution of the operating conditions under wet conditions. When the relative importance of all conditions was plotted (Fig. 2 (c)), the distribution was right-skewed owing to the larger number of ML models under wet conditions.

div.head: Theory-integrated ML models
div.p: The approach of combining data-driven and theory-based models can be classified as serial and hybrid integration [105]. In serial integration, each model is connected serially, whereas one structure of a model is combined with another for hybrid integration. A summary of the theory-integrated ML models is presented in Fig. 3. A few studies have combined data-driven and theory-based models to develop theory-integrated ML models for the thermochemical conversion process of biomass [38,71,88], but the approach and extent of theory-integration were different.

The simulation results of 2D CFD for biomass pyrolysis were used to develop a ML model [38] where the temperature and x/y coordinates were used as input variables. The simulation results at each CFD node were converted to output variables in the form of the time-averaged mass fractions of tar, gas, and biomass. Similarly, a reaction kinetic model of lignin pyrolysis was used to generate the data required for the development of ML models to predict the yield of solid and product gases and the distribution of functional groups in tars [71]. These types of ML model applications are called the reduced-order model (ROM), and they can be considered as the basic version of theory-integrated ML model or sequential integration. The benefit of using simulation data is that compared with experimental data, an abundant amount of data can be used for model training. Additionally, a certain degree of noise can be added to assess the robustness of trained models. Ji et al. [88] developed a theory-integrated ML model for kinetics based on the Arrhenius equation and an ANN (Fig. 4). The cellulose content, O 2 concentration, and reaction temperature were used as input variables, and the ANN model was trained to fit the thermogravimetric analysis results of the selected feedstocks (wood, grass, and crop). During the training procedure, the optimal number of neurons was determined based on the mean absolute error, indicating the number of immediate species that occurred in the reaction. The parameters from ML model were assumed to be a pre-exponential factor, activation energy, and non-exponential temperature-dependent factor [88]. The volatile gas emission rates were estimated based on the obtained kinetics. It should be noted that the ANN architecture was built based on the Arrhenius equation. This study is a good example of an explainable ANN model. The procedure for finding the optimal structure of the ANN was analogous to the procedure for finding an unknown reaction mechanism (Fig. 4). The number of hidden neurons in the hidden layer was analogous to the intermediate species that participated in the reaction but were not detected as products. These procedures can be applied to various thermochemical conversion processes of biomass with unknown mechanisms; therefore, this study is an excellent example of a theoryintegrated ML model.

div.head: Technoeconomic analysis (TEA) assisted by ML modelling
Technoeconomic analysis for biofuel conversion processes
div.p: Over the past decades, TEA has been regarded as one the most important tools for evaluati ng the economic aspects of chemical processes, including biofuel production processes. In add ition to energy or exergy analysis and life cycle assessment (LCA), the application of TEA h as increased exponentially. Classical TEA was performed using general-purpose software based on the process design. For the past 20 years, TEA has mostly been calculated through correl ations with process operation data, simulation results using commercial software, and process optimization results. Recently, it has evolved to the level of performing TEA directly or indir ectly by using ML techniques. Research results are beginning to emerge on energy optimizati on, environment, and profitability, and at the same time, integration of data-based technology into TEA. Among data-driven technologies, the genetic algorithm has been frequently used in TEA linked with process simulation and optimization; however, to date big data analysis, M L, ANN, and digital twin are few examples of the direct application of ML technologies.

div.head: Liquid biofuel
div.p: Marchetti et al. presented various alternatives to replace fossil fuel-based diesel fuel product ion [106]. Because raw materials encompass more than 80% of the production cost of conven tional fossil fuels, the development of technologies using low-cost raw materials generated in the animal and vegetable oil processing process has been proposed and economically evaluate d with TEA. Yaashikaa et al. [107] carried out an overall review of biodiesel production proc esses using algae. In particular, TEA and LCA were briefly mentioned using the parameters t hat affect algal growth and biodiesel productivity. Kushwaha et al. [108] performed a sustaina bility assessment for algal biodiesel production. Naveenkumar and Baskar [109] produced biod iesel from bio-oils by using a Zn-doped CaO-based catalyst. The sustainable biodiesel convers ion rate was 91.95%, with a green chemistry value of 0.873. Based on the experimental and calculation results, TEA of a 21,000 ton/year biodiesel production scale plant was performed with an annual biodiesel revenue of $15.2 M$/year and a payback period of approximately 1.

15 years. Huang et al. [110] presented a process for producing biodiesel from vegetable oil, i n particular, genetically modified lipid-producing sugarcane, and conducted an economic analys is. As the lipid content increased from 2% to 20%, the biodiesel production cost decreased fr om $0.89/L to $0.59/L, and the internal rate of return increased from 13.7% to 24.0%. Heo e t al. [111] compared different technologies of i) catalytic, ii) enzymatic, and iii) in situ transe sterification to produce microalgal biodiesel. After verifying the importance of the process vari ables through a global sensitivity analysis, TEA was performed. The biodiesel production cost s were in the order of catalytic ($4.77/kg), in situ ($9.92/kg), and enzymatic transesterification ($12.53/kg). Apostolakou et al. [112] performed TEA on the production of biodiesel -monoa lkyl esters of long-chain fatty acids obtained from lipid feedstock. After simulating the proces s of transesterification of vegetable oil and animal fat, TEA was performed according to the biodiesel production capacity. Bartling et al. [113] developed a process to fractionate lignocell ulose and converted lignin into a narrow product slate using a reductive catalytic fractionation technology. Research has been conducted to maximize the profit of high-value-added product s by minimizing the reaction pressure, reactant loading, and total amount of oil produced by reductive catalytic fractionation.

div.head: Gaseous biofuel
div.p: Masala et al. [114] installed a small-scale anaerobic digester with a capacity of 2477 t/year on an isolated island, and then analyzed and optimized three scenarios: (i) gas upgrading for the residential sector, (ii) upgrading for the transport sector, and (iii) electricity production in a combined heat and power plant. Akbulut et al. [115] performed TEA on biogas production in a small dairy farm in Turkey. Based on the operation data, net present value and energetic payback time were calculated. Additionally, the annual amounts of electricity, thermal energy, and CO 2 were compared. Vo et al. [116] presented three biogas-upgrading scenarios. The dig ester and amine scrubber (scenario 1), methanation of CO 2 and H 2 discharged from the scrub ber (scenario 2), and bio-methanation process that reacted biogas and hydrogen without an am ine scrubber (scenario 3) were modeled. The process was simulated, and TEA was subsequent ly performed. The CH 4 costs for Scenarios 1, 2, and 3 were 0.76, 1.50, and 1.43/m 3 , respecti vely. Rajendran and Murthy [117] reviewed the use of TEA and LCA for anaerobic digestion.

The TEAs and LCAs for biogas upgrading were calculated based on simulated processes usi ng operational data. Pääkkönen et al. [118] performed TEA for power to biogas based on the case in which the electricity price fluctuated. Renewable energy (excess electricity) is used to produce hydrogen, which then forms CH 4 by reacting with the CO 2 in biogas. Using this pro cess, up to 40% of electricity can be stored as biomethane. It was confirmed that profitability can be secured if the electrolyzer investment cost is reduced by 60-72% or the price of CH 4 produced is increased by 20-76%. Ferella et al. [119] performed TEA for upgrading biogas in the developed market. Maintaining the existing biogas plant and increasing the production of biomethane by introducing the pressure swing adsorption process were compared using TE A indicators such as internal rate of return, net present value, and discounted cash flow. Lee et al. [120] performed a TEA for biodiesel production based on biochar, and when the discou nt rate was 10%, the breakeven price was $1.55/kg, which is competitive with the existing pr ocess considering the carbon penalty and tax exemption.

div.head: ML-assisted TEA
div.p: ML techniques are being applied for TEA. Byun et al. [121] studied the technical, environ mental, and economic feasibility of a methanol-steam reforming process based on several tech no-economic parameters for H 2 production using an ML-based prediction model, as shown in Cheng and Luo [122] introduced ML techniques to perform an economic evaluation of alga e-derived biofuels from hydrothermal liquefaction. The ML model developed to predict biocru de energy yield incorporated (i) a biomass productivity model to show the correlation between lipid content and biomass productivity, (ii) a biomass production cost conclusion model to sh ow the correlation between biomass productivity and minimum selling price of biomass, and

(iii) biochemical composition. Olafasakin et al. [123] applied ML techniques to TEA for biom ass pyrolysis. However, unlike the above two studies, a ROM was utilized, where the chemic al reaction mechanism was identified by training with the results of the biomass pyrolysis ex periment (see Fig. 6). Technoeconomic analysis was performed based on the obtained ROM t hat resulted in biofuel production ranging from 65 to 130 gallons per ton of dry biomass, mi nimum biofuel selling price of $2.62-$5.43 per gallon, and global warming potential of -13.6
2 to 145 kg of CO 2 per MJ. These results suggest that ROM can facilitate rapid feedstock sc reening in biorefinery systems.
Fig. 6. Indirect TEA and LCA prediction based on process performance results from ML mod elling (adapted from [123]).

Vondra et al. [124] developed a descriptive economic model based on ML to evaluate the economics of evaporation systems in biogas plants and provided a heuristic method for decisi on makers. Using a new techno-economic model, the economic aspects of implementing the l atest vacuum evaporation system using the waste heat from the combined heat and power dev ice of a biogas plant were studied. To consider the real-world probability and robustness of t he analysis, Monte Carlo simulation techniques were used to generate more than 20,000 differ ent possibilities for implementing an evaporation system. Subsequently, an advantageous decisi on path was selected through a new methodology that utilized an ANN and a hyper-optimize d decision tree classifier.

div.head: Challenges and prospects
div.p: Although applications of the ML models for thermochemical biofuel conversion prediction have been extensively explored, these studies are still incapable of extending towards actual implementation and plant-scale optimization. Various reviews have emphasized the importance of datasets and theoryintegrated ML models in improving the ML models for practical applications. In the case of datasets, the importance of training with small datasets, multi-view data, uncertainty quantification, and data quality has been emphasized [125,126]. Although multi-view data include more comprehensive information for ML modelling [125], it could deteriorate the training procedure owing to the increased complexity of model structure. However, this can be overcome by using the compact architecture of ML model. It was shown that the compact form of neural network provided the best performance without increasing the number of neurons or complexity [127]. In addition, most studies used the composition of biomass that was summed up to 100%. Because there is an intercorrelation between compositions (or input variables), balance-related issues and the usage of independently measured compositions should be explored further [57]. The important aspects of data collection will be discussed in the following section. Theory-integrated ML models are growing in diverse fields because of their greater extrapolability and interpretability [128]. However, their application in biomass thermochemical conversion is still limited. In the next section, the possible integration of theory-based and ML models for predicting thermochemical conversion of biomass will be discussed.

div.head: Comprehensive data set
div.p: More comprehensive datasets should be created covering a wide range of feedstocks and operating conditions for developing models that are more generative to thermochemical conversion process of biomass. This can be achieved by creating a dataset following a standardized protocol. First, the characterization of biomass and operating conditions must be standardized. The composition of biomass is commonly analyzed using ultimate and proximate analyses. Some existing studies only provided one of these analyses, resulting in an incomplete dataset. Details of gas environment (air, CO 2 , or inert gases (Ar or N 2 )) should also be reported because of its significant influences towards the thermochemical conversion of biomass. A few studies have failed to provide necessary information on the gas environment.

Second, it is recommended to avoid using categorical input variables in the dataset. In some studies, the reactor type, catalyst type, and feedstock were included as categorical input variables for convenience. Such categorical variables can help ML models distinguish between different reactors, but they do not provide information about the extent to which the reactors differ. An ideal ML model should be able to predict all the output variables, differentiating reactor types and catalyst types to great accuracy and granularity. Defining categorical input variables using numerical variables can contribute to the improvement of the extrapolation of ML models. Fluidized and fixed beds are widely used for biomass thermochemical conversion and these reactors are commonly characterized by gas velocity and biomass density. If these reactors can be defined with common variables in a dataset, it will improve the performance of ML model by increasing the amount of available data [129]. Similarly, reactants (e.g., acetone or ethanol) with different effects on thermochemical conversion have also used as categorical input variables for ML modelling [76]. The dielectric constant of the reactants can be a candidate input variable and significantly influences the reaction kinetics in the thermochemical conversion of biomass. Because of the difficulty in generalizing their structures, both the catalyst and feedstock were normally represented as categorical input variables. The graph neural network (GNN) is based on graph-structure data, and it has become popular because it can predict various molecular properties by generalizing molecular representation [130]. A molecule can be represented as a topological graph where atoms and chemical bonds are considered nodes and edges, respectively [131].

Thus, atoms and bonds of catalysts and feedstocks can be generalized in graph-structure data, and GNN based on them can serve as a promising method for mitigating the adverse impact of categorical variables on ML modelling [131]. The GNN has been used to predict biodiesel combustion performance [131].

div.head: Integration of ML models with theory-based models
div.p: Combining ML models with a theory-based model can leverage their respective advantages [128].

The objective of this combination is usually to improve the predictive capability. Biomass thermochemical conversion processes are complicated and not fully understood. The proper integration of ML and theory-based models could be beneficial for solving chemical and biological complexity.

Aykol et al. summarized possible integration methods for other complicated systems [105]. Among the integration method suggested by Aykol et al. [105], parameter learning can be the one easily implementable. In such integration, complex behavior, such as reaction kinetics, can be modeled by a data-driven model, whereas relatively well-known transport phenomena are described by a theory-based model. For biomass conversion, not all reaction kinetics are understood, but the reaction kinetic parameters that explain the experimental data can be predicted by ML models. The utilization of the obtained kinetic parameters with a theory-based model or process simulation can improve the interpretability of the final result. In addition, GNNs have received increasing attention owing to their ability to capture interatomic potential or the relationship between molecular structure and properties.

The application of GNN to account for biomass structures would contribute to the generalization of various feedstocks. For example, the reaction kinetic parameters of pyrolysis could be modeled with GNN, and the kinetic parameters can be then utilized for process simulation. With such a GNN model, faster design of the thermochemical conversion process of new biomass can be achieved given the structure of the new feedstock can be rapidly characterized.

Another type of integrated modelling is theory-constrained ML, which is also known as physicsguided ML modelling. In general, the loss function (or error function) of a ML model is the summation (or mean) of the squared error between the target and prediction values. When a physics-guided loss term is added to the loss function, the ML model attempts to find the optimal weights and biases by reducing the physics-guided loss term [132]. Such physics-guided loss terms can encompass physics laws such as mass or energy conservation. In the case of syngas production, when physics-guided loss originating from the carbon balance before and after the conversion process is implemented, the biomass conversion process can be modelled with more rigorous mass balance.

The third is ML-accelerated theory-based modeling, in which nonlinear partial differential equations are rapidly solved by ML. This is a rapidly growing area, and there have been applications in diverse fields such as fluid mechanics and Schrodinger's equation [133]. The strength of the ML-accelerated theory-based modeling is based on the fact that a neural network is a universal approximator and includes automatic differentiation [105,134]. Thus, the neural network model can solve the underlying nonlinear partial differential equation, simultaneously satisfying the boundary conditions and physics laws. Solving partial differential equations in fluid dynamics is also important for the biomass thermochemical conversion process, in which a fluidized bed is widely utilized. In addition, thermochemical conversion via catalysis involves complex reaction kinetics. Thus, solving the governing equations of transport phenomena and reaction kinetics could contribute to the development of models for more sophisticated biomass thermochemical conversion processes in the future.

div.head: Integration of ML models with renewable energy aided systems
div.p: Integration of thermochemical bio-fuel conversion process with renewable energy systems have receive much attention with its high efficiency and environmental benefits [135]. Intermittency issues of renewable energy become additional consideration for these integrated systems. Thus, the complexity for optimization of such integrated system increased substantially. Besides being able to establish a comprehensive date set for biomass and respective thermochemical processes, the required data set should be expanded towards a much wider parameters while responded to the fluctuating energy condition during the thermochemical processes rapidly. The well-developed ML model that approximates the complex function can be used as a surrogate model to reduce the computational cost of optimizing the whole integrated process. When the optimization of the integrated systems is assessed for a given feedstock and renewable energy system, the choice of the thermochemical conversion process will be suggested by an advanced ML model. Either with various feedstocks blend to tackle the unstable supply of single feedstock or alternating between different energy sources. The corresponding operating conditions could be suggested by the ML model to produce biofuel stably and efficiently.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Recent development of ML models for thermochemical biofuel conversion processes were reviewed.

ML models have been developed to predict the yield and composition of biofuel products, as well as reaction kinetics. The predictive performance of ML models can be improved by increasing the number of data points, provided relevant hyperparameters are set properly. Although many experimental studies have been conducted, there is still a barrier attributed to the complex composition of biomass, preventing the utilization of all published data. In addition, the various types of reactors, catalysts, and reactants prevent the standardization of operating conditions and process designs for ML modelling. A comprehensive dataset that unifies various biomass characteristics and operating conditions and theoryintegrated ML models are highly desired and will promote the design and optimization of thermochemical conversion processes. Categorical input variables were better defined using numerical variables to improve the interpretability of input variables.
